hypotheses.title: ERC20RewardHook.claimRewards allows anyone to steal rewards via fake ISafe
hypotheses.description: The authorization check `isClaimer || ISafe(rewardedAddress).isOwner(msg.sender)` treats `rewardedAddress` as a trusted Safe contract. However, `rewardedAddress` is an arbitrary caller-supplied address. An attacker can deploy a malicious contract at any address that returns `true` from `isOwner(msg.sender)` (or simply pass an address they control that implements `isOwner` returning true), then call `claimRewards(attackerControlledAddress)` to drain any accrued rewards mapped to that address. Since rewards are keyed by arbitrary addresses (lenders and safes), an attacker who can predict or influence a lender address can claim on their behalf.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys contract `Fake` with `isOwner(address) returns (bool) { return true; }`. 2) Attacker calls `claimRewards(address(Fake))`. 3) The require passes because `ISafe(Fake).isOwner(msg.sender)` returns true. 4) `accruedRewards[Fake]` is transferred to `msg.sender`. If any rewards were accrued to that address (e.g., attacker arranged for `Fake` to be a lender in a rental), attacker steals them.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of accrued reward tokens belonging to any address that the attacker can make pass the `isOwner` check, including lender rewards.
hypotheses.recommendation: Do not trust arbitrary `rewardedAddress` as a Safe; instead require `msg.sender == rewardedAddress` OR verify `rewardedAddress` is a protocol-deployed safe via `STORE.deployedSafes(rewardedAddress) != 0` before calling `isOwner`.

hypotheses.title: Stop.sol settles payments and removes rentals after external calls
hypotheses.description: In `stopRent()`, the order of operations is: `_removeHooks` (external call to hook), `_reclaimRentedItems` (external call via safe module), `ESCRW.settlePayment(order)` (external ERC20 transfers), and only then `STORE.removeRentals(...)`. The order hash is not deleted from storage until after all external interactions. A malicious hook (whitelisted by admin, but attacker-controlled via `extraData`/target) or a malicious ERC20 payment token can reenter `stopRent()` with the same order before `removeRentals` executes, since `orders[orderHash]` is still true.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker creates a rental order with a hook they control (or a malicious ERC20 as payment). 2) When `stopRent` is called, `_removeHooks` or `_settlePayment` triggers the attacker's callback. 3) Callback reenters `stopRent(order)` with the same order. 4) `_validateRentalCanBeStoped` passes (still expired/lender), `_reclaimRentedItems` transfers assets again, `settlePayment` transfers ERC20s again, and `removeRentals` succeeds on the inner call. 5) Outer call then also runs `settlePayment` and `removeRentals` — double payment and double asset reclaim.
hypotheses.impact: Double-spend of escrowed ERC20 payments and double reclaim of rented NFTs/1155s; escrow insolvency and theft of other renters' deposits.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move `STORE.removeRentals` (and order-hash invalidation) before any external interaction, or add a reentrancy guard on `stopRent`/`stopRentBatch`.

hypotheses.title: ERC20RewardHook claims rewards via transfer to msg.sender not owner
hypotheses.description: The function requires msg.sender to be rewardedAddress or an owner of the safe, but then unconditionally transfers the rewards to msg.sender rather than to rewardedAddress. A safe owner who is not the lender can call claimRewards(safeAddress) and have the safe's accrued rewards sent to themselves rather than the safe.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker is an owner of a rental safe. 2. Safe accrues rewards in the hook. 3. Attacker calls claimRewards(safeAddress). 4. The check passes because ISafe(safeAddress).isOwner(attacker) is true. 5. The transfer sends tokens to attacker instead of to the safe.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of accrued reward tokens from the safe; incorrect accounting of rewards.
hypotheses.recommendation: Transfer rewards to rewardedAddress instead of msg.sender.

hypotheses.title: stopRentBatch settles all payments after per-order external calls
hypotheses.description: `stopRentBatch` loops over orders performing `_removeHooks` and `_reclaimRentedItems` (external calls) for each order, but defers `ESCRW.settlePaymentBatch(orders)` and `STORE.removeRentalsBatch(...)` until after the entire loop. During any hook callback or safe module execution, the order hashes are still active in storage and payments are still escrowed, so a reentrant call to `stopRent`/`stopRentBatch` on the same orders will succeed again.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker submits a batch containing an order with a malicious hook. 2) During `_removeHooks` for that order, the hook reenters `stopRent(order)` for the same order. 3) Inner call passes validation, reclaims assets, settles payment, and removes the order. 4) Outer batch continues and later calls `settlePaymentBatch` (paying again) and `removeRentalsBatch` (reverting or double-decrementing). If inner removal succeeds, outer `removeRentalsBatch` reverts on `orders[hash]` check — but the payment already went out twice.
hypotheses.impact: Duplicate ERC20 payouts from escrow; potential revert of the outer batch leaving inconsistent state; escrow insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove rentals from storage per-order inside the loop before any external call, or add a reentrancy guard.

hypotheses.title: Stop policy allows lender to stop PAY order at any time, renter loses pro-rata payment
hypotheses.description: In `_validateRentalCanBeStoped`, for PAY orders, if the stopper is the lender (`isLender` is true), the rental can be stopped at any time, even if the rental has not expired. This means a lender can stop a PAY order immediately after it starts, before the renter has had a chance to use the rented asset. When the lender stops the order, `_settlePayment` is called with `elapsedTime` and `totalTime`. If the rental is not over, the payment is settled pro-rata: the renter gets a portion of the payment based on the elapsed time, and the lender gets the rest. If the lender stops immediately, `elapsedTime` is very small, so the renter gets almost nothing, and the lender gets almost the full payment. This allows the lender to grief the renter by stopping the rental immediately, effectively taking the renter's payment without providing the rental service. The renter paid the full amount upfront, but the lender can stop the rental and keep most of the payment. This is an economic flaw: the lender has an incentive to stop the rental early and keep the payment, while the renter loses the rental and most of their payment. The renter cannot stop the rental themselves unless the rental has expired (for PAY orders, if the stopper is not the lender, the rental must have expired). So the renter is at the mercy of the lender.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Renter creates a PAY order and pays the full rental amount upfront. 2. Lender immediately calls `stopRent` on the order. 3. `_validateRentalCanBeStoped` allows it because the stopper is the lender. 4. `_settlePayment` calculates `elapsedTime` as a small number (e.g., 1 second) and `totalTime` as the full rental duration (e.g., 1 day). 5. The pro-rata split gives the renter a tiny fraction of the payment (e.g., 1/86400) and the lender the rest. 6. The renter loses the rental and almost all of their payment. 7. The lender keeps the payment and can rent the asset again.
hypotheses.impact: Renter loses the rental and most of their payment. Lender can grief renters and profit by stopping rentals immediately. This undermines the trust in the rental protocol and can lead to loss of funds for renters.
hypotheses.recommendation: For PAY orders, if the lender stops the rental before expiration, the renter should receive a full refund or a penalty should be applied to the lender. Alternatively, require that the lender can only stop after a minimum rental period, or that the renter must agree to the stop.

hypotheses.title: ERC20RewardHook uses transfer() which can silently fail or return false
hypotheses.description: `claimRewards` calls `rewardToken.transfer(msg.sender, withdrawAmount)` and ignores the boolean return value. For non-reverting ERC20s that return false on failure (e.g., some USDT-like or pausable tokens), the accrued rewards are zeroed out before the transfer, and a failed transfer leaves the user with nothing while the hook's accounting shows zero owed.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker triggers a condition where the reward token transfer returns false (e.g., token paused, blacklisted recipient, or insufficient hook balance due to prior mis-accounting). 2) `accruedRewards[rewardedAddress]` is set to 0 before the transfer. 3) Transfer returns false silently. 4) User's rewards are permanently lost.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent loss of accrued rewards for users; hook accounting diverges from actual token holdings.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use SafeERC20.safeTransfer or check the boolean return value and revert on failure.

hypotheses.title: RentPayload signature lacks nonce allowing replay of same payload
hypotheses.description: The RentPayload hash includes fulfillment, metadata, expiration, and intendedFulfiller, but no nonce or unique order identifier. The same signed payload can be reused to create multiple rental orders as long as the expiration has not passed and the fulfiller matches. Since `_rentFromZone` does not consume or invalidate the signature, an attacker who is the intended fulfiller can replay the same signed payload repeatedly.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a valid signed RentPayload (e.g., as the intended fulfiller). 2) Attacker submits the same payload/signature multiple times via Seaport `validateOrder` before expiration. 3) Each call creates a new rental order with the same terms, draining the lender's assets or escrow deposits repeatedly.
hypotheses.impact: Duplicate rental orders created from a single signature, causing repeated asset rentals, incorrect escrow accounting, and potential loss of lender assets.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include a unique nonce (or the Seaport order hash) in the RentPayload and track consumed nonces/order hashes in storage to prevent replay.

hypotheses.title: ERC20RewardHook claimRewards uses transfer not safeTransfer
hypotheses.description: The `claimRewards()` function uses `rewardToken.transfer()` instead of a safe transfer pattern. Some ERC20 tokens (e.g., USDT) do not return a boolean, causing the transfer to revert or silently fail. This can lock rewards permanently.
hypotheses.attackPath: If the reward token is a non-standard ERC20 (like USDT), users cannot claim rewards, and funds are frozen in the contract.
hypotheses.impact: Frozen funds, inability to claim rewards.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use OpenZeppelin's `SafeERC20.safeTransfer()` instead of `transfer()`.

hypotheses.title: Pro-rata rounding favors renter, drains escrow over many rentals
hypotheses.description: The pro-rata split adds a fixed +500 to the renter amount before dividing by 1000, which rounds the renter's share up rather than down. Because lenderAmount is derived as `amount - renterAmount`, the lender absorbs the rounding loss. Over many partial rentals, the escrow's tracked balanceOf is decremented by the full `item.amount` while the sum of transfers equals `amount`, so the rounding bias consistently shifts value from lender to renter.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (renter) creates many PAY orders with small payment amounts and short elapsed times. 2) Stops each rental early so pro-rata applies. 3) Each stop rounds renterAmount up by up to ~0.5 units, accumulating value at the lender's expense. 4) Attacker collects the inflated renter payouts.
hypotheses.impact: Systematic value transfer from lenders to renters; lenders receive less than their fair pro-rata share on every partial rental.
hypotheses.recommendation: Round the renter amount down (remove the +500 bump) so the protocol/lender retains the dust, or compute lenderAmount first with rounding down and derive renterAmount as the remainder.

hypotheses.title: Signer domain separator uses address(this) breaking cross-chain replay protection
hypotheses.description: The EIP-712 domain separator is computed with `address(this)` as the verifying contract. When the Create policy is deployed behind a proxy (or at different addresses on different chains), the same signed RentPayload can be replayed against a different deployment because the domain separator is bound to the implementation address rather than the proxy address. Additionally, `_DOMAIN_SEPARATOR` is cached at construction time and never recomputed if `block.chainid` changes (e.g., after a chain fork), so signatures remain valid across forked chains.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a valid signed RentPayload on chain A. 2) Attacker replays the same payload/signature on chain B where the Create policy is deployed at the same address (or where the domain separator collides). 3) Because the domain separator is derived from `address(this)` (implementation) and cached chainId, the recovered signer matches and the order is accepted.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized rental orders can be created on other chains/forks using signatures intended for a single chain, leading to unauthorized asset rentals and payment escrow deposits.
hypotheses.recommendation: Derive the domain separator using the proxy address (e.g., `address(this)` at proxy context) and recompute it dynamically when `block.chainid != _CHAIN_ID`, following EIP-712 best practices.

hypotheses.title: ERC1155RewardHook claimRewards allows anyone to drain rewards via fake safe
hypotheses.description: Same flaw as ERC20RewardHook: the access check `isClaimer || ISafe(rewardedAddress).isOwner(msg.sender)` does not verify that `rewardedAddress` is a protocol-deployed safe. An attacker can deploy a malicious contract that returns `true` from `isOwner(msg.sender)` and use it to claim rewards accrued to that contract. Since rewards are accrued to the `safe` address in `onStart`/`onStop`, an attacker who controls the `safe` (e.g., by being the renter) can accrue rewards to their malicious contract and then claim them. More importantly, if a legitimate safe has accrued rewards, an attacker cannot directly claim them unless they can make the safe return true for `isOwner(attacker)`, which requires being an owner. However, the lack of safe verification means any contract can be used as a claim proxy, and if the protocol ever accrues rewards to a non-safe address (e.g., due to a bug or misconfiguration), those rewards can be stolen.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker deploys malicious contract `M` with `isOwner(address) external pure returns (bool) { return true; }`. 2. Attacker ensures `accruedRewards[M]` is positive (e.g., by being the `safe` in a rental). 3. Attacker calls `claimRewards(M)`. 4. `ISafe(M).isOwner(msg.sender)` returns true. 5. Hook transfers `accruedRewards[M]` to `msg.sender`. 6. Attacker repeats for any address they control.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of reward tokens from any address that has accrued rewards and is not a legitimate Safe, or from a legitimate Safe if the attacker can make the Safe return true for `isOwner(attacker)`. In practice, the attacker can drain rewards from any address they control, but the real risk is that rewards accrued to a legitimate Safe can be stolen if the attacker can get the Safe to return true for `isOwner(attacker)` — which is not possible unless the attacker is an owner. However, the check is fundamentally flawed because it does not verify that `rewardedAddress` is a protocol-deployed safe, allowing any contract to be used as a claim proxy. This can lead to loss of rewards for legitimate users if an attacker can cause rewards to accrue to a malicious contract and then claim them.
hypotheses.recommendation: Verify that `rewardedAddress` is a protocol-deployed safe by checking `STORE.deployedSafes(rewardedAddress) != 0` before allowing claims, or restrict claims to the safe itself calling the function.

hypotheses.title: ERC20RewardHook/RewardHook claim uses unchecked ERC20 transfer return
hypotheses.description: rewardToken.transfer(msg.sender, withdrawAmount) return value is ignored. If the reward token returns false instead of reverting on failure, the accrued balance is zeroed but no tokens are sent, so the user's claim is silently lost and the tokens remain in the hook contract.
hypotheses.attackPath: Using a reward token with non-reverting false return (or a token that fails specific transfers) the hook zeroes accruedRewards[rewardedAddress] while transfer returns false. Subsequent claims return zero. An attacker cannot steal but accrual is wiped.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of claimable rewards for the affected address; incorrect accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use SafeERC20.safeTransfer or check the returned bool.

hypotheses.title: ERC1155RewardHook reward accrual uses currentAmount after partial stop, mis-splitting rewards
hypotheses.description: In `onStop`, rewards are accrued based on `currentAmount` (the total rented amount before decrement) for the entire `blocksToReward` window, then `currentAmount` is decremented by `amount`. If multiple rentals of the same asset exist with different lenders, the rewards for the elapsed blocks are attributed to the lender of the stopping rental using the full `currentAmount`, over-crediting that lender and under-crediting others. The same issue exists in `onStart` when `currentAmount` is incremented after accrual.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Two lenders rent the same ERC1155 asset to two different safes. 2) One renter stops their rental. 3) `onStop` accrues rewards for the full `currentAmount` (both rentals) to the stopping rental's lender. 4) The other lender loses their share of rewards for that period.
hypotheses.impact: Rewards are misallocated between lenders; some lenders receive more, others less than their fair share.
hypotheses.recommendation: Accrue rewards per-rental using the amount associated with each specific rental, or track per-lender/per-safe accrual separately.

hypotheses.title: Reclaimer transfers ERC721/ERC1155 unconditionally, reverting stop for non-standard or reverting receivers
hypotheses.description: `reclaimRentalOrder` calls `IERC721(...).safeTransferFrom` and `IERC1155(...).safeTransferFrom` to the lender. For ERC721/1155, `safeTransferFrom` invokes `onERC721Received`/`onERC1155Received` on the lender if it is a contract. If the lender is a contract that does not implement the receiver interface (or a relayer-contract that reverts), the whole stop flow reverts, and the order can never be stopped — locking the rented assets inside the rental safe indefinitely since the guard blocks transfers while the rental is active.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (as renter) creates a PAY order where the lender is a contract that reverts on `onERC721Received` (or fails the receiver check). 2) The order becomes active and the guard blocklists the asset. 3) At stop time, `_reclaimRentedItems` calls `reclaimRentalOrder`, which does `safeTransferFrom` and reverts; neither renter nor lender can stop the order, so the asset + payment remain stuck.
hypotheses.impact: Rented asset is permanently frozen in the safe; lender payment is stuck in the escrow; the entire order becomes unstoppable (state remains `orders[hash]=true`, `rentedAssets[id]!=0`).
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `transferFrom` (non-safe variant) for ERC721/1155 when reclaiming to the lender, or wrap the safe transfer with a try/catch that falls back to unsafe transfer.

hypotheses.title: Fee taken on payment but skim uses true balance, allowing fee double-count
hypotheses.description: When a fee is active, `_decreaseDeposit` reduces `balanceOf[token]` by the full `item.amount`, but only `paymentAmount = item.amount - fee` is transferred out. The fee remains in the contract as an untracked surplus. `skim()` computes `trueBalance - syncedBalance` and sends the entire difference to the admin. If a token with transfer fees or a rebasing token is used, or if multiple orders settle between skims, the surplus accounting can drift and the skim amount may not equal the actual accumulated fees, potentially skimming funds that belong to pending settlements.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker uses a fee-on-transfer ERC20 as the payment token. 2) On settlement, `_decreaseDeposit` reduces balanceOf by the nominal amount, but the actual received amount was less. 3) `skim()` computes trueBalance - syncedBalance, which now includes both fees and the shortfall from transfer fees, and sends it to the admin. 4) Pending settlements for other orders may be under-collateralized.
hypotheses.impact: Escrow can become insolvent for other pending rentals; fees and principal are commingled and mis-skimmed.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track fees in a separate `fees[token]` accumulator and skim only that, or measure actual received amounts on deposit and use those for balanceOf.

hypotheses.title: skim() reverts or underflows when trueBalance < syncedBalance (fee-on-transfer tokens)
hypotheses.description: `skim` computes `skimmedBalance = trueBalance - syncedBalance`. If a fee-on-transfer or rebasing token is used, the actual balance can be less than the synced `balanceOf`, causing an underflow revert and permanently blocking fee collection. Additionally, if the token rebases upward, the extra balance is treated as fees and skimmed, potentially taking funds that belong to pending settlements.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker uses a rebasing token as payment. 2) Token rebases downward, making trueBalance < syncedBalance. 3) `skim()` reverts on underflow, blocking admin fee collection. 4) Alternatively, token rebases upward and the surplus is skimmed as fees, draining pending settlement funds.
hypotheses.impact: Fees cannot be collected (DoS) or pending settlement funds are incorrectly skimmed as fees.
hypotheses.recommendation: Guard against underflow and only skim amounts explicitly tracked as fees, not the raw balance difference.

hypotheses.title: ERC20RewardHook uses block.number for time-based rewards
hypotheses.description: The reward accrual uses `block.number` to calculate elapsed time, but `rewardPerBlock` is a fixed rate per block. On chains with variable block times or during network congestion, the actual time elapsed may not match the block count, leading to incorrect reward distribution. More critically, if the hook is deployed on a chain where block times change significantly, rewards can be over- or under-accrued.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker can manipulate block production timing (e.g., via validator collusion or on L2s with variable block times) to accrue more rewards than intended per unit time, then claim them via `claimRewards()`.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect reward accounting, potential over-distribution of reward tokens leading to insolvency of the reward pool.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `block.timestamp` instead of `block.number` for time-based reward calculations, or ensure the reward rate is explicitly per-block and block times are stable.

hypotheses.title: PaymentEscrow.settlePayment decreases deposit before transfer, but batch can be reentered via ERC20 callback
hypotheses.description: `_settlePayment` calls `_decreaseDeposit(item.token, item.amount)` before `_safeTransfer`. This is correct CEI ordering for the escrow's own balance. However, `_safeTransfer` uses a low-level `call` to the token, which for ERC-777 or hook-enabled tokens invokes `tokensToSend`/`tokensReceived` callbacks. During the callback, the attacker can reenter `settlePayment` for a *different* order that shares the same token, or call `skim` (if they have permission — they don't) or `increaseDeposit` (permissioned). The real risk: a malicious token can reenter `settlePaymentBatch` for the same batch, and since `_decreaseDeposit` already ran for the current item but not for subsequent items, the attacker can cause the batch to process items out of order or double-process. More concretely, the token callback can call `settlePayment` for an order whose `balanceOf[token]` is still sufficient, draining escrow for orders that haven't been settled yet.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a malicious ERC20 used as payment in a rental. 2) When `settlePayment` is called, `_safeTransfer` invokes the token's callback. 3) Callback reenters `settlePayment` for another order using the same token (attacker is lender/renter on both). 4) The second settlement decreases `balanceOf[token]` and transfers out funds. 5) Outer settlement continues; if `balanceOf[token]` underflows, the outer call reverts, but the inner transfer already succeeded — or if balances are sufficient, both settle, draining escrow beyond the intended amount for the attacker's orders.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of escrowed ERC20 funds belonging to other rentals; escrow insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a reentrancy guard to `settlePayment`/`settlePaymentBatch`, or use a pull-pattern where recipients withdraw after all state updates.

hypotheses.title: ERC1155 reward hook claimRewards always reverts on zero accrued rewards
hypotheses.description: `claimRewards()` unconditionally calls `rewardToken.safeTransferFrom(address(this), msg.sender, rewardTokenId, withdrawAmount, "")` even when `withdrawAmount == 0`. Most ERC1155 implementations revert or emit non-compliant behavior on a zero-value transfer, so any caller (or safe owner) whose `accruedRewards[rewardedAddress]` is zero will have the call revert, preventing them from ever resetting/using the claim flow. The same pattern is present in ERC20RewardHook (which uses `transfer` with 0, still generally succeeds but relies on non-reverting token).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `onStart`/`onStop` or otherwise interacts such that a safe/lender accrues zero rewards (e.g., first-time rent). 2) Attacker (or owner) then calls `claimRewards(victimSafe)` where victim's `accruedRewards == 0`. 3) Transfer with zero amount reverts for many ERC1155 tokens, blocking that path. More generally, any token whose `safeTransferFrom` reverts on zero traps the claim flow.
hypotheses.impact: Claim flow permanently reverts for affected addresses if rewardToken reverts on zero-value transfers, causing partial denial of service and preventing the user from clearing/using state through the documented path.
hypotheses.recommendation: Skip the transfer when `withdrawAmount == 0` (early `return`) before calling `safeTransferFrom`/`transfer`.

hypotheses.title: `_safeTransfer` reverts for zero-amount ERC20 settlements, blocking stop on pro-rata splits
hypotheses.description: In pro-rata splits, `_calculatePaymentProRata` can produce a zero `renterAmount` or zero `lenderAmount` when elapsed time is very small/large relative to total time (elapsed→0 yields renterAmount 0; elapsed≈total yields lenderAmount near 0). `_settlePaymentProRata` then unconditionally calls `_safeTransfer` for both amounts, including the zero one. For USDT-style ERC20s that revert on zero, the whole `stopRent` transaction reverts, so the order cannot be stopped and the rented item + remaining escrow funds stay locked.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (as lender) creates a PAY order using a non-standard ERC20 that reverts on zero transfers. 2) Attacker (as lender) immediately calls `stopRent` right after rental start so elapsedTime is tiny; renterAmount rounds to 0. 3) `_settlePaymentProRata` calls `_safeTransfer(token, renter, 0)` which reverts, blocking the stop and the reclaim of the rented ERC721/1155.
hypotheses.impact: The rented asset remains permanently held by the safe (guard blocks transfers, stop reverts), and the lender's payment is stuck in escrow. No recovery path exists since stop is the only settlement entrypoint.
hypotheses.recommendation: Skip transfers when the computed amount is zero (both in human-readable and fallback paths).

hypotheses.title: ECDSA.recover accepts malleable signatures without low-s check
hypotheses.description: The code uses OpenZeppelin's `ECDSA.recover`, which does enforce low-s and v-value checks in recent versions, but the recovered signer is only checked against `kernel.hasRole(signer, toRole("CREATE_SIGNER"))`. If the kernel role is granted to an address derived from a malleable signature variant, an attacker could produce an alternative valid signature for the same digest. More importantly, the code does not bind the signature to the specific Seaport order hash, so a signature valid for one order can be reused for another order with the same payload hash.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a signed payload. 2) Attacker constructs a different Seaport order whose `zoneParams.extraData` decodes to the same RentPayload (same fulfillment, metadata, expiration, intendedFulfiller). 3) The signature recovers to the authorized signer and the order is accepted, even though the Seaport order differs.
hypotheses.impact: Signature reuse across different Seaport orders, allowing unauthorized order creation with attacker-chosen offer/consideration items.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind the signed payload to the Seaport order hash (include `zoneParams.orderHash` in the signed digest) so a signature is only valid for one specific order.

hypotheses.title: ERC20RewardHook onStart/onStop reward calculation uses currentAmount before update, allowing reward inflation
hypotheses.description: In `onStart`, the reward calculation uses `currentAmount` (the amount before adding the new `amount`). This means that if a rental is started with a large `amount`, the rewards for the period since the last accrual are calculated based on the old (smaller) amount, not the new amount. Conversely, in `onStop`, the reward calculation uses `currentAmount` (the amount before subtracting `amount`), which is correct for the period the asset was rented. However, the issue is that `onStart` updates `lastRewardBlock` to `block.number` after calculating rewards, but the new `amount` is added after the reward calculation. This means that for the period between the last accrual and the start of the new rental, the rewards are calculated based on the old amount, which is correct. But if multiple rentals are started in the same block, the `lastRewardBlock` is updated to the same block, and the `currentAmount` is updated, so subsequent starts in the same block will calculate zero blocks to reward. This is not an exploit per se, but it can lead to unfair distribution if a user starts a rental with a large amount and then immediately stops it, as the rewards for the period they held the asset are calculated based on the amount they held, which is correct. The real issue is that the reward calculation does not account for the fact that the `amount` is added after the reward calculation, so if a user starts a rental with a large amount, the rewards for the period since the last accrual are based on the old amount, which is correct. However, if a user starts a rental and then stops it in the same block, the `blocksToReward` will be zero, so no rewards are accrued. This is not an exploit. The more significant issue is that the reward calculation uses `currentAmount` which is the total amount rented by all renters for that asset hash. If multiple renters rent the same asset (same safe, token, identifier), the `currentAmount` is the sum of all their amounts. When one renter stops, the reward is calculated based on the total `currentAmount`, and then split between the lender and the renter who is stopping. This means that the renter who stops gets a share of rewards that were accrued while other renters were also holding the asset. This is a fairness issue: a renter who stops early can claim rewards that were accrued during a period when other renters were also holding the asset, effectively stealing rewards from them. The `onStop` function calculates rewards based on `currentAmount` (total rented) and then subtracts the stopping renter's `amount`. The rewards are split between the lender and the stopping renter. The remaining renters do not get their share of the rewards for that period; instead, the stopping renter gets a share based on the total amount, which includes the other renters' amounts. This means the stopping renter can claim more than their fair share. This is a real economic flaw.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker (renter A) rents a small amount of an asset. 2. Another renter B rents a large amount of the same asset (same safe, token, identifier). 3. After some blocks, renter A stops their rental. 4. In `onStop`, `currentAmount` is the sum of A's and B's amounts. The rewards for the blocks since last accrual are calculated based on this total. 5. The rewards are split: half to lender, half to renter A. 6. Renter A receives a share of rewards that were accrued due to B's large amount, even though A only held a small amount. 7. Renter B, when they stop later, will have their rewards calculated based on the remaining amount (after A stopped), so they lose the rewards that A stole.
hypotheses.impact: Unfair distribution of rewards: a renter who stops early can claim a disproportionate share of rewards accrued while other renters were holding the same asset. This can be exploited to steal rewards from other renters. The lender also gets a share based on the total amount, which may be correct, but the renter's share is inflated.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track rewards per renter individually, or calculate rewards based on the renter's own amount, not the total `currentAmount`. Alternatively, accrue rewards to a pool and distribute proportionally to each renter's contribution.

hypotheses.title: ERC1155RewardHook.onStop underflow when amount exceeds stored
hypotheses.description: `rentInfo[assetHash].amount -= amount;` will underflow and revert if `amount` passed by the stop policy exceeds the stored amount. Since `onStop` is called by the stop policy with the order's item amount, a mismatch between the amount recorded at start and the amount at stop (e.g., due to a partial stop or a manipulated order) causes a revert, blocking the stop flow. More importantly, the hook trusts the caller-supplied `amount` without verifying it matches the stored `currentAmount`, so a malicious stop policy (or a bug) could pass a smaller amount and leave residual accounting.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A rental is started with amount X. 2) A stop is attempted with amount Y > X (e.g., via a crafted order). 3) `amount -= Y` underflows and reverts, blocking the stop. Alternatively, passing Y < X leaves stale accounting.
hypotheses.impact: DoS on stop flow or incorrect reward accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Validate `amount == currentAmount` (or cap the subtraction) before updating `rentInfo[assetHash].amount`.

hypotheses.title: Create._addHooks calls hooks before order hash is finalized in storage
hypotheses.description: In `_rentFromZone`, `STORE.addRentals(orderHash, ...)` and `ESCRW.increaseDeposit(...)` are called, then `_addHooks(...)` invokes external `IHook(target).onStart(...)`. The hook is called after storage is updated, which is correct ordering, but the hook can reenter `validateOrder` (via Seaport) or call `ESCRW.increaseDeposit`/`STORE.addRentals` if it has permissions. More critically, a malicious hook can call `stopRent` on the just-created order (if it can satisfy the stop validation) before `_emitRentalOrderStarted` — but the order hash is already in storage, so `stopRent` would succeed and remove it, then the outer `_rentFromZone` continues and emits the start event for an already-stopped order. The hook is whitelisted by admin, but the hook's `extraData` is attacker-controlled and the hook itself may be a legitimate contract with a reentrancy surface.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker crafts an order with a hook that, in `onStart`, calls `Stop.stopRent(order)` for the same order (the order hash is already in `STORE.orders`). 2) `stopRent` validates (BASE order not expired → reverts; PAY order with lender=attacker → passes), reclaims assets, settles payment, removes rentals. 3) Outer `_rentFromZone` continues, emits `RentalOrderStarted` for a non-existent order. 4) Off-chain indexers and the protocol's own accounting are now inconsistent; the renter's payment was settled but the order is marked started.
hypotheses.impact: Inconsistent protocol state; event/state desync; potential for double-settlement if the order is later stopped again (it won't be, since removed) — but the emitted event misleads indexers and could enable further exploits.
hypotheses.recommendation: Emit the start event before calling hooks, or add a reentrancy guard on `validateOrder`/`_rentFromZone`.

hypotheses.title: Create2Deployer salt check uses bytes20(salt) but generateSaltWithSender shifts incorrectly
hypotheses.description: `generateSaltWithSender` uses `shl(0x60, sender)` to place the 20-byte address into the high bytes of a bytes32, and `shr(0xA0, data)` to place 12 bytes of data into the low bytes. However, `deploy` checks `address(bytes20(salt)) != msg.sender`, which reads the first 20 bytes of the salt. The shift `shl(0x60, sender)` shifts the 20-byte address left by 96 bits, placing it in the top 20 bytes — this matches `bytes20(salt)`. But the `data` portion is shifted right by 160 bits, which for a bytes12 value (96 bits) will zero out the data entirely, making the salt deterministic per sender and losing the intended uniqueness. This allows two different deployments by the same sender to collide on the same salt if the data is not properly encoded.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or any sender) calls `generateSaltWithSender` with different `data` values. 2) Due to the incorrect shift, the resulting salts are identical for the same sender. 3) The second `deploy` call reverts with `AlreadyDeployed`, or worse, if the attacker can front-run with a crafted salt, they can occupy the intended address.
hypotheses.impact: Deployment address collisions, denial of service for legitimate deployments, or front-running of CREATE2 deployments.
hypotheses.recommendation: Correct the shift amounts: use `shl(0x60, sender)` for the address and `shl(0x50, data)` (or appropriate shift) for the 12-byte data, ensuring the full salt is populated correctly.

hypotheses.title: ERC1155RewardHook ERC165 supportsInterface omits IERC1155Receiver
hypotheses.description: The contract implements IERC1155Receiver and returns the transfer-acceptance magic values, but supportsInterface only claims IERC165 and IERC1155. Any caller of rewardToken.safeTransferFrom from this hook will depend on the reward token calling onERC1155Received back; if the reward token uses ERC165 to check on the receiver's supportsInterface for IERC1155Receiver before transferring, the transfer may be rejected, permanently locking accrued reward tokens in this contract.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable by an untrusted actor; the failure mode is triggered when the configured reward token performs an ERC165 check.
hypotheses.impact: Accrued rewards may be non-claimable / stuck.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add interfaceId == type(IERC1155Receiver).interfaceId to supportsInterface.

hypotheses.title: stopRentBatch emits derived hash not seaport order hash
hypotheses.description: In stopRentBatch the loop emits RentalOrderStopped with _deriveRentalOrderHash(orders[i]) as the first argument, while stopRent emits the actual order.seaportOrderHash. The two code paths use inconsistent identifiers for the same event, misleading off-chain indexing and any consumer that correlates stops by seaportOrderHash.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable by an untrusted actor — off-chain observability inconsistency only.
hypotheses.impact: Misleading event log; potential off-chain accounting mismatch.
hypotheses.recommendation: Emit order.seaportOrderHash in stopRentBatch as in stopRent.

hypotheses.title: ERC20RewardHook.onStart/onStop trust caller-supplied lenderShare
hypotheses.description: The `lenderShare` is decoded from `data` supplied by the create policy (which is derived from the order's extraData). While the create policy is trusted, the hook does not validate that the `lender` in `RevenueShare` matches the actual lender of the order. A malicious order creator could set an arbitrary `lender` address in the extraData, causing rewards to be accrued to an address they control rather than the real lender. The hook has no way to verify the lender independently.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker creates a rental order with `extraData` encoding `RevenueShare{ lender: attacker, lenderShare: 100 }`. 2) On start, rewards accrue to attacker. 3) Attacker claims rewards.
hypotheses.impact: Misappropriation of lender rewards.
hypotheses.recommendation: Pass the actual lender address from the order into the hook (e.g., via a trusted parameter) rather than decoding it from untrusted extraData, or validate it against the order.

hypotheses.title: ERC20RewardHook lenderShare check allows 100% to lender, renter gets zero
hypotheses.description: The check `revenueShare.lenderShare <= 100` permits a 100% lender share, leaving `renterAccruedRewards = latestAccruedRewards - lenderAccruedRewards = 0`. While this may be intentional, the rounding of `lenderAccruedRewards = (latestAccruedRewards * lenderShare) / 100` truncates, so for lenderShare < 100 the renter receives the truncated dust. This is a minor accounting asymmetry but not exploitable by an untrusted actor without controlling the hook data.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable by an untrusted actor; requires the order creator to set lenderShare.
hypotheses.impact: Minor dust misallocation between lender and renter.
hypotheses.recommendation: Document the rounding direction or compute renter share first and derive lender share as remainder.

hypotheses.title: PaymentEscrow pro-rata calculation can round in renter's favor
hypotheses.description: The pro-rata calculation adds 500 before dividing by 1000 to round to nearest. This rounding can favor the renter over the lender by up to 0.0005 * amount. While small, repeated across many orders this can accumulate. More importantly, if `elapsedTime` is very small relative to `totalTime`, the rounding can result in renterAmount being larger than expected.
hypotheses.attackPath: A renter can repeatedly create and stop rentals at very short elapsed times to exploit rounding in their favor, extracting small amounts from lenders each time.
hypotheses.impact: Gradual loss of funds from lenders to renters due to rounding errors.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a more precise rounding method or round in favor of the lender to prevent value extraction.

hypotheses.title: ERC1155RewardHook claimRewards uses safeTransferFrom without checking return
hypotheses.description: The `claimRewards()` function calls `rewardToken.safeTransferFrom()` but does not check the return value. While `safeTransferFrom` should revert on failure, some non-compliant ERC1155 implementations may return false without reverting, leading to silent failures.
hypotheses.attackPath: If the reward token is a non-compliant ERC1155, users may not receive rewards despite the transaction succeeding.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of rewards for users.
hypotheses.recommendation: Check the return value of `safeTransferFrom()` or use a wrapper that reverts on false.

hypotheses.title: ERC1155RewardHook.claimRewards transfers before checking success
hypotheses.description: `claimRewards` zeroes `accruedRewards[rewardedAddress]` then calls `rewardToken.safeTransferFrom(...)`. The ERC1155 `safeTransferFrom` invokes `onERC1155Received` on the recipient (`msg.sender`), which is an external callback. Because `accruedRewards` is zeroed before the call, direct reentrancy on the same address is safe, but the callback can reenter `claimRewards` for a *different* `rewardedAddress` that the attacker also controls (e.g., a safe they own), and the `ISafe(rewardedAddress).isOwner(msg.sender)` check is performed against the reentered address. If the attacker controls multiple safes, they can chain claims; more importantly, the callback runs while the hook's state is mid-update for other addresses.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker owns two safes A and B with accrued rewards. 2) Calls `claimRewards(A)`; during `safeTransferFrom` callback, reenters `claimRewards(B)`. 3) Both claims proceed; no double-spend of the same address, but the callback can also call `onStart`/`onStop` if the attacker is the create/stop policy — not applicable here. The main risk is that the callback can invoke `claimRewards` on a safe whose `isOwner` check passes for `msg.sender` (the hook itself during callback), which is not the case. Limited impact.
hypotheses.impact: No direct fund loss demonstrated; potential for unexpected state interactions if reward token is malicious.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a reentrancy guard or use a pull-pattern with a per-address claim flag.

hypotheses.title: ERC20RewardHook.claimRewards uses transfer instead of safeTransfer and lacks reentrancy guard
hypotheses.description: `claimRewards` sets `accruedRewards[rewardedAddress] = 0` before calling `rewardToken.transfer(msg.sender, withdrawAmount)`. While this follows checks-effects-interactions, the use of `transfer` instead of `safeTransfer` means tokens that do not return a bool (or return false) will not be handled correctly, and a malicious reward token could reenter `claimRewards` or other hook functions. Additionally, the function does not verify that `rewardedAddress` is a legitimate safe or lender, allowing any address to be passed as long as `msg.sender` is the owner of that address (or the address itself).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a malicious reward token that reenters `claimRewards` on transfer. 2) Attacker calls `claimRewards` with their own address. 3) During the transfer, the malicious token reenters `claimRewards`, but since `accruedRewards` was already zeroed, the reentrant call withdraws nothing — however, the attacker can still exploit the lack of safeTransfer to cause the transfer to silently fail while rewards are zeroed.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of accrued rewards if the token transfer silently fails, or reentrancy issues if the reward token is malicious.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `SafeERC20.safeTransfer` and add a reentrancy guard to `claimRewards`.

hypotheses.title: ERC1155RewardHook.claimRewards allows anyone to claim for a safe they own, but no validation of rewardedAddress
hypotheses.description: `claimRewards` checks `isClaimer || ISafe(rewardedAddress).isOwner(msg.sender)`. If `rewardedAddress` is not a Safe contract, the call to `ISafe(rewardedAddress).isOwner` will revert or return false. More critically, if `rewardedAddress` is a Safe that the attacker owns, they can claim rewards accrued to that Safe. However, the hook accrues rewards to `revenueShare.lender` and `safe` (the rental wallet). An attacker who is an owner of a Safe can claim rewards that were accrued to the Safe, but the lender's rewards are only claimable by the lender. The issue is that `rewardedAddress` is not validated against the actual accrued rewards mapping — any address with a nonzero `accruedRewards` can be claimed by its owner, which is intended, but the lack of a check that `rewardedAddress` is a protocol-deployed safe or a known lender allows an attacker to claim rewards for an arbitrary address they control.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a contract that implements `isOwner` to return true for the attacker. 2) Attacker calls `claimRewards` with `rewardedAddress` set to that contract. 3) The check passes and the attacker claims any rewards accrued to that address.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized claiming of rewards if an attacker can get rewards accrued to an address they control.
hypotheses.recommendation: Validate that `rewardedAddress` is either a protocol-deployed safe or a known lender, and consider using a pull-based pattern with explicit recipient validation.
